quote: Further, I winsorize the distribution at the 95th percentile to account for top-coding in the CPS. In practice, I estimate the quantile function on an equally spaced grid of 95 points between $[1\times 10^{-6},0.95+1\times 10^{-6}]$, where the $1\times 10^{-6}$ offset ensures I work on a compact subset of $[0,1]$ as required by the theoretical results.
feedback: Winsorizing at the 95th percentile replaces all mass above the cutoff with a single value, which makes the right tail of every state's quantile function flat and, in particular, makes the *average* quantile function flat (zero derivative) as q approaches 0.95. But Assumption L4 requires the average quantile function to be strictly increasing with derivative bounded below by a strictly positive constant kappa, and L4 is exactly what delivers the identity Hadamard derivative in the proofs of Theorem 4 and Lemma A-9 (i.e., the claim that the Fréchet projection is asymptotically inactive and the bootstrap bands are valid). Worse, the only uniformly significant effects in the application are at the 85th-95th percentiles, i.e., precisely the region where winsorizing threatens L4. This is a substantive internal tension: the headline result lives in the part of the distribution where the maintained assumption underpinning the inference is most fragile. I recommend (i) re-running on a sub-interval [a,b] safely bounded away from 0.95 (e.g., b=0.9) and verifying the top-decile result survives; (ii) using a less destructive top-coding correction (e.g., a parametric Pareto tail or cell-means imputation) so the average quantile function remains strictly increasing; and (iii) stating explicitly how winsorizing interacts with L4 and what happens to the limiting distribution when L4 fails on a sub-interval.
gloss_en: Winsorizing at the 95th percentile flattens the average quantile function, threatening Assumption L4 exactly where the significant top-decile effects are claimed.

quote:
$\sqrt{nh}\left(\hat{m}_{\pm,\oplus,p}-m_{\pm}\right)\leadsto\mathbb{G}_{H\pm}(\cdot,1),$

where $\mathbb{G}_{H\pm}$ is the *same* zero-mean Gaussian process as in Theorem 1.
feedback: Theorem 4 establishes that the Fréchet estimator and the pointwise local-polynomial estimator have the *identical* limiting Gaussian law, and Lemma A-9 shows their difference is o_p((nh)^{-1/2}). This result, while elegant, undercuts much of the paper's framing. The text repeatedly asserts the Fréchet estimator is 'preferred' due to 'superior finite-sample performance' and a 'no-regret' property (Lemma 2) guaranteeing it is 'always closer to the truth.' But Lemma 2 only states a weak (non-strict) inequality that holds for an arbitrary fixed input curve; it does not establish a strict variance reduction, and asymptotically the two estimators are indistinguishable to first order. Consequently the finite-sample gains in Figures 3-4 are asserted but never theoretically characterized — the reader cannot tell whether they reflect a genuine second-order efficiency improvement, the monotonicity constraint binding in small samples, or the single-bandwidth choice. There is also a circularity worth flagging: the IMSE-optimal bandwidth for the Fréchet estimator is justified *only* by appeal to this first-order equivalence (Section 2.7, A-4.2.2), so the bandwidth is optimal for the local-polynomial estimator, not demonstrably for the object actually used. I recommend either deriving the second-order (e.g., higher-order MSE) difference that formalizes the finite-sample advantage, or substantially softening the 'preferred/superior' language to 'asymptotically equivalent, with a monotonicity guarantee and a single bandwidth.'
gloss_en: The two estimators share an identical limiting law, so the claimed finite-sample superiority of the Fréchet estimator is asserted but never theoretically characterized.

quote: (i) $\{(Y_i, T_i, X_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ are i.i.d. copies of a random element $(Y, T, X)$ defined on a probability space $(\Omega^x, \mathcal{F}^x, P^x)$.
feedback: The entire asymptotic theory and the multiplier bootstrap rest on Assumption L1(i): the across-unit observations are i.i.d. In the empirical application the unit of observation is a state-year, and the sample is gubernatorial elections from 1984-2010 (356 state-years). The same state appears repeatedly (roughly six to seven times over the window), state income distributions are strongly serially correlated, and state-level shocks induce within-state dependence across years. L1(i) is therefore violated in exactly the application used to showcase the method. The clustered-RDD literature the paper itself cites (Bartalotti and Brummet 2017; Lee and Card 2008) exists precisely for this reason, and the paper acknowledges in Section 1 that clustering 'does not carry through' to quantile effects — yet the application proceeds as if state-years were independent. Note Table A-1 clusters the *canonical* RD comparison at the state(-year) level but the R3D bootstrap bands are not clustered at all. This is a concrete inference-validity problem that likely makes the reported uniform bands too narrow. I recommend (i) extending the multiplier bootstrap to a cluster/block design that resamples whole states, (ii) reporting how the top-decile significance changes under state-clustered inference, and (iii) stating the dependence structure under which the i.i.d.-based theory remains an adequate approximation.
gloss_en: The i.i.d. assumption L1(i) is violated by repeated, serially correlated state-years in the application, and the R3D bootstrap bands are not clustered.

feedback: The condition that empirical quantile functions are asymptotically negligible is Assumption Q1, whose binding requirement is sqrt(nh) * max_{1<=i<=n} r_{n_i} -> 0. Because it is the *maximum* over units, the constraint is governed by the *smallest* within-group sample, not the average: with r_{n_i} on the order of n_i^{-1/2}, Q1 requires sqrt(nh)/sqrt(min_i n_i) -> 0, i.e., the worst-sampled group must grow strictly faster than nh. In the CPS application n is small (356 state-years), h=0.22 so nh is roughly 78, and CPS state-year cells for small states can be modest and do not grow with n in any controlled way. The paper never reports the distribution of n_i, never identifies min_i n_i, and never verifies Q1. If the smallest cells are of order a few hundred or fewer, the plug-in error from empirical quantiles is *not* first-order negligible and the bands understate uncertainty. I recommend reporting the within-group sample-size distribution (especially the minimum among states near the cutoff), checking the implied sqrt(nh)*max r_{n_i} quantity directly, and — if it is not small — either adding a within-group sampling-error term to the variance or trimming small cells.
gloss_en: Assumption Q1 binds on the smallest within-group sample via the maximum, is never verified, and is plausibly violated by small CPS state-year cells.

quote: Note: this table shows simulated acceptance probabilities for the $95\%$ uniform confidence bands ("Unif. CIs", probability of coverage), uniform homogeneity test ("Homogen."), and uniform treatment nullity test ("Nullity") presented in Section 2.6 for various sample sizes, where $n = n_i$ for all simulations, with $n_i$ the sample size for the empirical quantile function.
feedback: Setting n = n_i throughout the Monte Carlo means the across-group sample size and the within-group sample size are always equal and grow together. This design never isolates the two-level structure that is the paper's entire conceptual contribution, and in particular it never stresses the empirical-quantile regime (Section 3.3.1, Assumption Q1) where n_i is small relative to n — which is exactly the regime the CPS application inhabits. As a result, the simulations cannot speak to whether the plug-in of empirical quantile functions is innocuous in realistic small-cell settings, nor to whether coverage degrades when within-group sampling noise is non-negligible. I recommend adding a simulation grid that varies n and n_i independently (e.g., fixing modest n_i in {50,100,200} while growing n, and vice versa), reporting coverage of the uniform bands in each cell. This would directly validate Proposition 2 and Corollary 3, which currently have no targeted simulation support.
gloss_en: Simulations fix n = n_i throughout, so they never test the small-within-group regime that the empirical-quantile theory and the application actually require.

quote: The identification assumption is that the outcome of interest evolves smoothly with the party’s vote share in a small window around the 50% electoral threshold that puts the party in power.
feedback: The application is a close-election RDD, a design with a well-known vulnerability to sorting/manipulation near the 50% threshold (the Caughey and Sekhon 2011 critique of close U.S. elections), yet the paper presents no validity diagnostics. There is no manipulation/density test at the cutoff (the McCrary 2008 or Cattaneo-Jansson-Ma test), even though Assumption I2 is a density-continuity condition that such a test is designed to probe; there is no covariate-balance or pre-determined-characteristics check across the threshold; and there is no placebo-cutoff or placebo-outcome falsification (beyond the election-year-income check, which addresses reverse causality but not sorting). For a paper whose empirical contribution is a causal claim about partisan control, these standard RD validity checks are essential, and their distributional analogues would also showcase the method (e.g., testing for a jump in the *covariate* distributions at the cutoff using the same R3D bands). I recommend adding a density/manipulation test, covariate balance at the cutoff, and at least one placebo-cutoff exercise.
gloss_en: The close-election design reports no manipulation/density test, covariate balance, or placebo-cutoff checks, despite known sorting concerns and an explicit density assumption.

feedback: The rate conditions in K2, and their interaction with the dual use of the polynomial order, need clarification and possibly correction. First, nh^2 -> infinity is stronger than the usual local-polynomial requirement nh -> infinity; it should be stated why the stronger rate is needed (it appears to come from the covariance/U-statistic control borrowed from Chiang et al. 2019) and whether nh -> infinity would suffice. Second, the undersmoothing condition nh^{2p+3} -> 0 is written in terms of the *estimation* order p, but the paper's bias-correction strategy (Remark 7 of Calonico et al. 2014) estimates with order p while choosing the bandwidth to be MSE-optimal for a *lower* pilot order s < p; the relevant undersmoothing condition for valid bias-corrected inference is usually stated relative to s, not p, and the two are not interchangeable. Readers cannot currently verify that the bandwidth actually used in the simulations and application (quadratic estimation, p=2, with linear-MSE bandwidths, s=1) simultaneously satisfies nh^2 -> infinity and nh^{2p+3} -> 0 under the chosen rate. Please (i) reconcile the roles of p and s in the rate conditions, (ii) confirm the conditions are mutually compatible for the (s,p)=(1,2) configuration used throughout, and (iii) verify the chosen IMSE bandwidth rate lies in the admissible window.
gloss_en: The bandwidth rate conditions are stated in the estimation order p but the bias-correction uses a lower pilot order s, leaving the admissible-rate logic unverified.

feedback: The LAQTE is defined as the difference of two Wasserstein barycenter quantile functions, m_1(q) - m_0(q). While each m_t is a legitimate average quantile function, their *difference* generally is not the quantile function of any distribution, and — more importantly — it does not correspond to a quantile treatment effect for any unit or to the quantile function of a treatment-effect distribution. The paper sells this object as letting one 'study what happens to the outcome distribution of the average unit,' but because the expectation is taken inside the quantile (an average of quantile functions across the distribution-of-distributions), the resulting curve mixes within-unit distributional shape with across-unit heterogeneity in a way that has no rank-preservation or counterfactual-distribution interpretation at the unit level. This matters for how applied readers will read Figure 6: 'income falls 1.5x the poverty line at the top decile' is a statement about the average of top-decile quantiles across states, not about any state's actual top earners or about a coherent counterfactual income distribution. I recommend a dedicated paragraph delimiting precisely what the LAQTE does and does not identify (e.g., contrasting it explicitly with the quantile of the barycenter and with unit-level QTEs), and tempering the 'average unit' / 'average distribution' language accordingly.
gloss_en: The LAQTE is a difference of barycenter quantiles with no unit-level or counterfactual-distribution causal interpretation, yet is framed as the effect on the 'average unit.'

quote: Taken together, these results suggest a classical equality–efficiency trade–off under Democratic governorship, with some redistribution of income achieved at the cost of a loss of income for upper-income earners *(Okun, 1975)*.
feedback: The 'equality-efficiency trade-off' interpretation is an overreach relative to what is estimated. Efficiency is never measured: the paper observes that top-decile incomes fall and bottom-quantile incomes rise (with only the top decile uniformly significant), and a negative average effect (-0.646). A fall in top incomes is not the same as a loss of aggregate output or efficiency — it is consistent with redistribution, tax-induced relocation of reported income, changes in the composition of who is captured in the CPS, or out-migration of high earners (only partially addressed by the cross-state-migration robustness in Figure A-8, which cannot capture income shifting or non-mover behavioral responses). Invoking Okun's deadweight-loss framing requires a welfare or output measure the design does not provide. I recommend reframing the finding descriptively ('Democratic control is associated with lower top incomes and a compressed distribution, with no significant change at the bottom') and either dropping the efficiency-loss claim or supporting it with an explicit output/efficiency outcome.
gloss_en: Calling the result an 'equality-efficiency trade-off' overreaches: efficiency/output is never measured, and falling top incomes need not imply an efficiency loss.

quote: The year 2010 marked a structural breakpoint in state politics (see e.g. the sharp increase in state-level polarization documented in *Shor et al. (2022)*) due to the significant Republican gains from the Tea Party wave and the subsequent implementation of the Affordable Care Act (ACA).
feedback: Ending the sample in 2010 is given a substantive justification, but the choice raises a specification-search concern that should be addressed head-on. The paper states elsewhere that 'the effects remain similar when including post-2010 data' but with reduced precision and magnitude (Figure A-6), which means the chosen window is also the one that maximizes statistical significance of the headline result. Because the cutoff date is a researcher degree of freedom and the post-2010 attenuation is acknowledged, a skeptical reader will worry that significance is partly an artifact of window selection rather than a stable structural effect. I recommend (i) showing the full time series of the top-decile estimate and its band as the end-year is varied (a sensitivity curve), (ii) reporting results for the full available sample as the primary specification with the pre-2010 window as a robustness restriction (not the reverse), and (iii) if possible, formally testing for the claimed 2010 structural break rather than asserting it.
gloss_en: The 2010 end-year is a researcher degree of freedom that also maximizes significance, raising a specification-search concern not directly addressed.

quote: The slight undercoverage in small samples is expected insofar as the estimators are only asymptotically unbiased, as also illustrated in Figure 3.
feedback: The coverage numbers in Table 2 do not behave the way 'slight, vanishing small-sample undercoverage' would predict. For the uniform bands the acceptance probability rises only from about 92.5% (n=500) to 94.2-94.4% (n=2000) and remains short of the 95% nominal level even at the largest sample size, across both DGPs and both estimators. A bias that vanishes asymptotically should drive coverage toward nominal as n grows; coverage that plateaus near 94% suggests a more systematic source — for example, the bias-corrected variance not fully accounting for the variability of the bias estimate (the very issue Calonico et al. 2018 address, and which the application patches with an ad hoc rule-of-thumb correction), or finite-grid/critical-value approximation error in the multiplier bootstrap. The flat plateau, not the small-sample level, is what needs explaining. I recommend (i) extending the simulation to larger n to show coverage actually reaches 95%, (ii) reporting coverage with and without the Calonico et al. 2018 correction in the *simulations* (not only the application), and (iii) diagnosing whether the residual gap is bias- or variance-driven.
gloss_en: Uniform-band coverage plateaus near 94% even at n=2000 rather than converging to nominal 95%, suggesting a systematic rather than vanishing small-sample problem.

feedback: The fuzzy-design complier apparatus is under-specified and partly degenerate. As written, the 'Indefinites' set is {T^1=T^0} minus {T^1=T^0 in {0,1}}; since T takes values in {0,1}, every omega with T^1=T^0 already has the common value in {0,1}, so this difference is the empty set and the subsequent assumption P(Indefinites)=0 is vacuous (or the intended object — defiers, or non-monotone types — is mislabeled). Beyond the notation, the conceptual issue is more important: in the standard fuzzy RD, compliance is defined on the scalar treatment T, but here the outcome under treatment is an entire *distribution*, and the Fuzzy LAQTE in Definition 2 conditions on the complier event C. Selection into compliance can be correlated with the *shape* of a unit's outcome distribution (e.g., states whose governor's party flips at the margin may differ systematically in their income distributions), so the conditional average quantile over compliers need not have a clean LATE-style interpretation, and monotonicity (I3.3) is a restriction on T that says nothing about distributional selection. I recommend (i) fixing the Indefinites/defiers definition, (ii) stating monotonicity and the exclusion restriction precisely for the distribution-valued setting, and (iii) discussing what the complier-conditioned barycenter difference identifies and under what additional restrictions it is policy-relevant.
gloss_en: The fuzzy-design 'Indefinites' set is empty as written, and the distribution-valued complier/LATE interpretation under monotonicity is not properly justified.
